title: Immersion
role_in_argument: Densest-citation chapter in the volume. Surveys and critiques the pre-Calleja immersion + presence literature; enumerates the four conceptual challenges the rest of the book undertakes to resolve; previews the 'toward a solution' move that Chapter 3 (PIM) implements. Carries the volume's sole Heidegger citation (p.21) and is the conceptual hinge between IG-01 (Games Beyond Games) and IG-03 (PIM).

outline.heading: (Unnamed opening — VR/cyberpunk trope; two-term problem)
outline.summary: Sets the scene with the cyberpunk image of the prone body neurally jacked into VR (Wachowski + Wachowski 1999 cited as cultural intertext). Locates the academic-public discourse around two flagship terms: presence (Minsky 1980) and immersion (Murray 1998). Cites Grau 2003 (illusion-spaces back to Roman villas, 60 BC), Bazin 1967 [1946] ('myth of total cinema'), and Sutherland 1965/1968 ('the Ultimate Display'). Flags that consensus exists on importance but not on meaning, with the term immersion particularly awkward because it has been applied across non-ergodic media (painting, literature, cinema) whose engagement is qualitatively distinct from game environments. Names the cite-cluster of authors who have flagged the definitional confusion (Slater 2003; Waterworth + Waterworth 2003; Ermi + Mäyrä 2005) and those who insist on the experiential phenomenon's centrality to games (King + Krzywinska 2006; Tamborini + Skalski 2006; Brown + Cairns 2004; Jennett et al. 2008).

outline.heading: Presence and Immersion in Presence Theory
outline.summary: Traces the genealogy of presence-theory from Minsky's 1980 'telepresence' (teleoperation) through the founding of the journal Presence (1992) and the Sheridan-vs-Held+Durlach terminological fork (virtual-presence-as-distinct vs. telepresence-as-umbrella). Critiques the dominant Held+Durlach equivalence-assumption via Ijsselsteijn + Riva (2003) — argues equating physical-environment and mediated-environment stimuli is not merely terminological but ontological, and sidelines the designed/contrived nature of virtual environments. Develops the chapter's central critique of fidelity-determinism through Mel Slater's quadraphonic-orchestra example (Slater 2003), arguing that the 'form/content' partition Slater proposes ignores the role of interpretation, agency, and prior experience in constituting presence. Heidegger 1993 cited (p.21) for the everyday-vs-disrupted comportment distinction: when interpretive schemata fail we must 'actively think about what we are doing'. Closes by laying out the conflicting Slater+Wilbur 1997 (immersion-as-technology, presence-as-response) vs. Witmer+Singer 1998 (immersion-as-psychological-state, presence-as-involvement-plus-immersion) inversion; introduces Calleja's own positive claim — that the player in a virtual world is 'anchored, via her avatar', so the game-world reacts to her, a structural feature absent in literature, film, or private imagining.

outline.heading: Presence as Transparency
outline.summary: Treats Lombard + Ditton (1997) — six characterizations of presence (social richness / realism / transportation / immersion / social actor within / medium as social actor) reduced to the common thread 'perceptual illusion of non-mediation', with perceptual vs. psychological immersion as a sub-division. Cross-links to Bolter + Grusin (1999) 'logic of transparent immediacy' — distinguished from Lombard + Ditton's formulation but operating in the same theoretical neighborhood. Grants the transparency-of-medium claim is essential but insufficient. Demonstrates the inadequacy of Lombard+Ditton when operationalized via McMahan's (2003) Myst III: Exile analysis, which Calleja reads as a 'descriptive listing of game features classified according to Lombard and Ditton's six categories' — pigeonholing without yielding game-specific affordances. Quotes McMahan's social-realism passage to show that her diagnostic claims (elevators, zeppelins, page-turning) apply trivially to most digital games in the genre. Concludes that McMahan also drifts: she treats immersion as a form of involvement, diverging from presence-theory's transportation-connotations — a drift Calleja flags as symptomatic of the broader confusion.

outline.heading: Presence and Immersion in Game Studies
outline.summary: The chapter's longest subsection. Catalogues industrial-promotional uses of 'immersive' (Conan / Need for Speed Underground 2 / Half-Life), critiques the 'idealization of total immersion' as cyberpunk-Neo-romanticism. Builds the chapter's load-bearing absorption-vs-transportation distinction by working through Salen + Zimmerman (2003) and their endorsement (via Gorfinkel and Laramée) of Tetris-as-immersive — which Calleja partially endorses (the critique of mimetic-realism imperative is sound) and partially rejects (it conflates absorption with transportation by sidelining spatiality). Names the absorption-sense (OED 'absorption in some condition, action, interest, etc.') and the transportation-sense (Murray 1998; Ryan 2001; Laurel 1991; Steuer 1992; Tamborini+Skalski 2006; Ijsselsteijn 2004; Ijsselsteijn+Riva 2003; Waterworth+Waterworth 2003; Slater 2003 — note the heterogeneous coalition behind transportation). Figure 2.1 (p.27) — Tetris (Pajitnov 1985) paired with Half-Life 2 (Valve 2004) — visually anchors the distinction: Tetris affords no spatial habitation (player controls blocks without single-location embodiment; environment shown in totality on one screen); Half-Life 2 affords spatial habitation through avatar-anchoring + continuous navigation. Bejewelled (PopCap 2001) and Eliss (Thirion 2009) extend the non-habitable class; strategy games (controlling 'multiple miniatures or a collective unit such as a nation') are treated likewise — player engages map rather than inhabited space. Quotes Ryan (2001) on representation-of-space as defining feature of immersion ('not an ocean but a textual world'). Then traverses three more critiques: (a) Dovey + Kennedy (2006) — immersion/engagement used interchangeably; gameplay 'time economy' framing usable but term is too unspecific; (b) Douglas + Hargadon (2001) — immersion-vs-engagement based on critical stance (within-frame schema vs. extra-textual perspective), praised for attentional-continuum recognition, critiqued for the Balzac-Dickens-Krantz-equals-Space-Invaders move that collapses ergodic vs. non-ergodic; (c) Brown + Cairns (2004) — three-degree ladder engagement → engrossment → total immersion, productively flagged as continuum of involvement BUT mixed-metaphor (levels 1-2 = absorption, level 3 = transportation), exacerbating the very confusion they aimed to resolve; Cairns et al. (2006) follow-on study inherits the flaw; (d) Ermi + Mäyrä (2005) — multidimensional gameplay-experience model (sensory / challenge-based / imaginative immersion); applauded for multidimensionality and medium-specificity recognition, critiqued for empirically deriving 'immersion' from child interviews (collapses academic-technical sense into colloquial sense).

outline.heading: The Four Challenges
outline.summary: Synthesizes the chapter's diagnostic in four enumerated challenges: (1) immersion as absorption versus immersion as transportation — the two-metaphor problem; (2) immersion in non-ergodic media — distinct phenomenon from ergodic media's; (3) technological determinism — fidelity does not deliver presence; (4) monolithic perspectives on immersion — must be a continuum of attentional intensity, not a binary on/off switch; each of (1)-(2) is constituted by multiple experiential phenomena, not a single one to be measured. Closes by anticipating that 'whichever term we use ... or propose a new metaphor, as will be done here, these challenges need to be addressed before progress can be made.'

outline.heading: Toward a Solution
outline.summary: Brief hinge subsection bridging to Ch.3. Re-locates the two terms within their originating disciplines (technologists/media psychologists/HCI use 'presence'; humanists and later social scientists use 'immersion'). States that both terms have suffered from varied application; advances toward 'establishment of clear and precise terms' as the necessary first step — the work IG-03's Player Involvement Model undertakes to do. This is the chapter's structural transition: lit-review terminates and the volume's positive theoretical apparatus begins.

concepts.label: immersion as absorption
concepts.definition: Use of 'immersion' to denote the OED-grade 'absorption in some condition, action, interest, etc.' — applicable in principle to gardening, cooking, crossword puzzles, or Tetris; pre-virtual-environment, content-agnostic, non-medium-specific.

concepts.label: immersion as transportation
concepts.definition: Use of 'immersion' to denote being-present-in-another-place; the spatially-anchored, medium-specific sense Calleja preserves for game environments. Carries the Murray/Ryan/Laurel/presence-theory heritage.

concepts.label: presence (umbrella sense)
concepts.definition: Sensation of being inside a virtual environment; descended from Minsky's telepresence; in dominant usage drifted to cover both virtual and physical environments (Held+Durlach onward).

concepts.label: telepresence (Minsky 1980)
concepts.definition: Sense of inhabiting a distant physical space achieved through operator-action plus video/audio/haptic feedback in teleoperation; the originating term from which 'presence' is derived.

concepts.label: virtual presence (Sheridan 1992)
concepts.definition: Sheridan's terminological reservation: telepresence for teleoperation only; virtual-presence for VEs. Later abandoned as the umbrella 'presence' subsumed both.

concepts.label: perceptual illusion of non-mediation (Lombard + Ditton)
concepts.definition: Common thread distilled from six characterizations of presence; foregrounds interface-erasure as the unifying experiential signature.

concepts.label: logic of transparent immediacy (Bolter + Grusin)
concepts.definition: Aesthetic logic of interface-erasure: form and content combine to deliver the appearance of unmediated access. Distinct from but co-extensive with Lombard+Ditton's perceptual-illusion-of-non-mediation.

concepts.label: perceptual vs. psychological immersion (Lombard + Ditton sub-distinction)
concepts.definition: Sub-partition under 'presence as immersion': perceptual = hardware effect on senses (≈ Slater+Wilbur immersion); psychological = absorption-metaphor (≈ Brown+Cairns / Douglas+Hargadon / Ermi+Mäyrä / Salen+Zimmerman / Jennett et al.).

concepts.label: immersive fallacy (Salen + Zimmerman)
concepts.definition: The claim that media-pleasure resides in sensual transportation into illusory simulated reality so complete the frame falls away. Salen+Zimmerman attack the corresponding mimetic-realism imperative in design; Calleja partially endorses the attack, partially rejects the resulting Tetris-immersibility move.

concepts.label: engagement / engrossment / total-immersion ladder (Brown + Cairns 2004)
concepts.definition: Three-degree typology of increasing involvement intensity; productively flags continuum-of-attention but mixes metaphors (levels 1-2 absorption, level 3 transportation).

concepts.label: sensory / challenge-based / imaginative immersion (Ermi + Mäyrä 2005)
concepts.definition: Multidimensional gameplay-experience model: sensory (audiovisual), challenge-based (mental+motor skill), imaginative (catchall for character-identification, narrative, world-engagement). Empirically grounded in child-interview data.

concepts.label: fidelity-determinism (critique)
concepts.definition: Calleja's name for the position (exemplified by Slater 2003's quadraphonic-orchestra example) that hardware-fidelity determines presence regardless of interpretation, agency, or prior experience. Rejected — the technology cannot in itself create presence.

concepts.label: technological determinism (challenge 3)
concepts.definition: Generalization of fidelity-determinism: that the qualities of the technology determine the experiences they afford. Calleja resists: a bigger screen and higher fidelity may aid focus but do not guarantee presence.

concepts.label: monolithic perspective on immersion (challenge 4)
concepts.definition: Treatment of immersion (whether as absorption or transportation) as a single, discoverable, measurable experience rather than as a composite of experiential phenomena distributed on a continuum of attentional intensity.

concepts.label: ergodic vs. non-ergodic media (deployed without explicit Aarseth cite)
concepts.definition: Distinction (originating in Aarseth 1997, deployed in Calleja's chapter without an in-chapter Aarseth cite) between media that require nontrivial player effort to traverse (games) and media that do not (literature, film, painting). Load-bearing for challenge 2.

concepts.label: anchoring of the player via avatar
concepts.definition: The structural feature whereby the player occupies a specific location in the game world via her avatar, and that location is recognized and reacted-to by the game-world and its entities — including, in multiplayer cases, other players. Differentiates game-immersion from book-imagination.

concepts.label: metaphorically habitable environment
concepts.definition: A player's assimilation of the game world into gameplay as something to be dwelt-in (proto-incorporation). Half-Life 2 affords this; Tetris, Bejewelled, Eliss, and strategy games (engaged 'as map rather than as spatial environment') do not.

concepts.label: attentional continuum (vs. on/off binary)
concepts.definition: Position that involvement spans a graded continuum from conscious attention to unconscious involvement; later operationalized as Ch.3's macro/micro temporal-phase distinction. Originates in Calleja's reading of Douglas+Hargadon's continuum claim.

concepts.label: involvement as prerequisite to presence/immersion
concepts.definition: Position (derived charitably from Brown+Cairns's ladder) that increasing levels of involvement are prerequisite to immersion-as-transportation. Calleja extracts this from the otherwise-flawed B+C account and carries it into Ch.3 as a positive seed.

concepts.label: terminological promiscuity / definitional confusion
concepts.definition: Calleja's name for the field-wide problem: the same terms used incompatibly, contradictorily, or interchangeably (presence/immersion/engagement/absorption) across overlapping research communities; the work of Ch.2 is to expose this and Ch.3 to remediate it.

concepts.label: the four conceptual challenges (canonical enumeration)
concepts.definition: Calleja's canonical diagnostic: (1) absorption-vs-transportation; (2) ergodic-vs-non-ergodic; (3) technological determinism; (4) monolithic perspectives. Becomes the diagnostic checklist any immersion claim must answer.

concepts.label: noetic vs. extranoetic habitation
concepts.definition: Distinction Calleja draws (using 'noetic' to describe purely imagined presence, 'extranoetic habitation' to describe game-world habitation that is reacted to by the system). The reader of a literary work imagining a world remains noetic; the player of a game environment that recognizes her location is extranoetic.

concepts.label: Slater's form/content partition (rejected)
concepts.definition: Slater's distinction (presence = form; engagement-with-content = something else) by which a presence-inducing VE can have uninvolving content. Calleja rejects: form/content cannot be cleanly partitioned because interpretive apparatus and prior lived experience constitute the sense of presence itself.

concepts.label: interpretive comportment (the Heidegger p.21 moment)
concepts.definition: Calleja's Heidegger-anchored claim that everyday interactions are mediated by internalized knowledge ('most interactions ... are possible because we have an internalized knowledge of how various aspects of that environment work'); only when interpretation fails do we become 'critically removed' and must 'actively think about what we are doing' (Heidegger 1993). The SOLE Heidegger-anchored text-moment in the entire volume.

concepts.label: presence-stretching critique (the 'entirely noetic phenomenon' charge)
concepts.definition: Calleja's charge that presence-research, by extending the term to non-ergodic media (Witmer+Singer; Schubert+Crusius 2002; Gysbers et al. 2004; Marsh 2003; Lee 2004), has stretched presence to cover 'what is essentially an entirely noetic phenomenon' — abandoning the system-recognition feature that originally motivated the term.

concepts.label: critique-and-rescue pattern (Calleja's response-type taxonomy)
concepts.definition: Analytic kind: Calleja critiques a prior author's specific formulation but preserves and reconstitutes the underlying intuition under a new vocabulary in Ch.10 (paradigm: Murray's transportation-via-imagination → incorporation's habitation-metaphor). Distinct from displace-and-replace and critique-and-supersede patterns.

positions.label: Position: the absorption-vs-transportation conflation is a definitional confusion the field must resolve
positions.claim: Use of 'immersion' to denote both general involvement-in-medium and transportation-to-another-reality without disambiguation impedes theoretical progress; the OED-grade absorption sense and the virtual-environment transportation sense must be terminologically separated.

positions.label: Position: immersion in ergodic vs. non-ergodic media is not the same phenomenon
positions.claim: Game environments afford forms of engagement qualitatively distinct from those of literature, film, or painting; extending immersion-concepts across this divide collapses analytically essential distinctions (centrally, the system-recognition feature).

positions.label: Position: technological determinism (and the fidelity-determinism sub-position) must be rejected
positions.claim: The qualities of the technology do not determine the experiences it affords; interpretation, agency, and prior lived experience are constitutive of presence and immersion, not merely modulatory.

positions.label: Position: immersion must be analyzed as a composite of experiential phenomena on a continuum, not a single binary-measurable state
positions.claim: Whether construed as absorption or transportation, the phenomenon is constituted by multiple experiential components arrayed on a continuum of attentional intensity; monolithic accounts must give way to multidimensional, graded analyses.

positions.label: Position: avatar-anchoring + system-reactivity is the structural differentia of game-environment presence
positions.claim: The game-world's reaction to the player's specific in-world location, mediated by avatar-embodiment, is the structural feature that distinguishes virtual-environment presence from imaginative noetic presence in books or films. This is the seed of Ch.10 incorporation.

pre_calleja_immersion_models.full_citation: Murray, Janet Horowitz. 1998. Hamlet on the Holodeck: The Future of Narrative in Cyberspace. Cambridge, MA: MIT Press.
pre_calleja_immersion_models.model_label: deep immersion / immersion-as-transportation (sensation of being transported into an elaborately simulated place)
pre_calleja_immersion_models.calleja_critique_summary: Calleja treats Murray as the named ancestor of the transportation-sense rather than as a foil. Her account is critiqued only insofar as it is the chief carrier of the transportation-metaphor whose vocabulary Calleja proposes to replace; the underlying experiential intuition (being-transported-into-a-place) is preserved and reconstituted in Ch.10 as incorporation's habitation-metaphor.
pre_calleja_immersion_models.propagation_note_from_IG10: Volume p.172 (IG-10 synthesis) confirms Murray is ABSORBED-NOT-REFUSED: the transportation-metaphor is reconstituted under 'incorporation'. The Ch.2 critique is targeted at Murray's specific vocabulary (deep immersion / transportation-via-imagination) but the underlying intuition is preserved. This is the asymmetric pattern that distinguishes Calleja's treatment of Murray from his treatment of presence-theory.

pre_calleja_immersion_models.full_citation: Ryan, Marie-Laure. 2001. Narrative as Virtual Reality: Immersion and Interactivity in Literature and Electronic Media. Baltimore: Johns Hopkins University Press.
pre_calleja_immersion_models.model_label: spatial / textual-world immersion (representation-of-space as defining feature; 'not an ocean but a textual world')
pre_calleja_immersion_models.calleja_critique_summary: Ryan is quoted approvingly at p.31-32 to defend the centrality of spatiality against the Gorfinkel-Salen-Zimmerman Tetris-immersibility move. Calleja appropriates Ryan's representation-of-space claim as evidence for the transportation-sense's medium-specific footing. No frontal critique; Ryan operates as a co-belligerent on the transportation side of the absorption-vs-transportation partition.
pre_calleja_immersion_models.propagation_note_from_IG10: Ryan's spatiality-as-defining-feature is preserved and operationalized in IG-05 Spatial Involvement as a full PIM dimension. Like Murray, Ryan is a transportation-side ancestor whose underlying intuition incorporation absorbs rather than refuses.

pre_calleja_immersion_models.full_citation_a: Slater, Mel, and S. Wilbur. 1997. A Framework for Immersive Virtual Environments (FIVE): Speculations on the Role of Presence in Virtual Environments. Presence 6 (6): 603-616.
pre_calleja_immersion_models.full_citation_b: Slater, Mel. 2003. A Note on Presence Terminology. Available from http://presence-connect.com.
pre_calleja_immersion_models.calleja_critique_summary: Sustained critique. Slater is the chapter's primary fidelity-determinism foil: his quadraphonic-orchestra example (Slater 2003, 607) is read as exemplifying the position that hardware-fidelity creates presence regardless of interpretive engagement. The form/content partition (presence = form; engagement = content) is rejected because form and content cannot be cleanly separated — interpretive apparatus and prior lived experience are constitutive of presence itself.
pre_calleja_immersion_models.propagation_note_from_IG10: Slater's immersion-as-technology vocabulary is wholly displaced. Incorporation does not preserve the immersion-as-hardware-property sense. Slater is the paradigm of the displace-and-replace pattern Calleja applies across presence-theory.

pre_calleja_immersion_models.full_citation: Witmer, B. G., and M. J. Singer. 1998. Measuring Presence in Virtual Environments: A Presence Questionnaire. Presence 7 (3): 225-240.
pre_calleja_immersion_models.model_label: immersion as psychological state of envelopment; presence = involvement + immersion
pre_calleja_immersion_models.calleja_critique_summary: Witmer + Singer's immersion-as-psychological-envelopment inverts Slater+Wilbur's immersion-as-hardware. Calleja treats this inversion as symptomatic of the presence-field's terminological confusion: two of the field's flagship accounts use the same terms with opposed meanings. The Witmer+Singer collapse of immersion into psychological-state also extends presence to non-ergodic media (one of the moves the chapter critiques as stretching presence to cover an 'entirely noetic phenomenon').
pre_calleja_immersion_models.propagation_note_from_IG10: Witmer+Singer's presence-questionnaire psychometrics are not reconstituted in incorporation; the entire framing (presence as quantifiable psychological state) is displaced by Calleja's six-dimensional involvement model.

pre_calleja_immersion_models.full_citation: Lombard, Matthew, and Theresa Ditton. 1997. At the Heart of It All: The Concept of Presence. Journal of Computer-Mediated Communication 3 (2).
pre_calleja_immersion_models.model_label: six characterizations of presence reduced to 'perceptual illusion of non-mediation'; perceptual vs. psychological immersion sub-distinction
pre_calleja_immersion_models.calleja_critique_summary: Praised for the synthetic move (six characterizations distilled to a single common thread) but critiqued via McMahan's failed Myst III application — when operationalized for analysis, the six-categories framework reduces to feature-list pigeonholing that fails to elucidate game-specific affordances. The perceptual/psychological sub-distinction is granted as theoretically useful but inherits the absorption-vs-transportation confusion (psychological immersion ≈ absorption-sense).
pre_calleja_immersion_models.propagation_note_from_IG10: Lombard+Ditton's framework is displaced; perceptual-illusion-of-non-mediation is not preserved in incorporation, which works from habitation rather than from interface-erasure.

pre_calleja_immersion_models.full_citation: McMahan, Alison. 2003. Immersion, Engagement and Presence: A Method for Analyzing 3-D Video Games. In The Video Game Theory Reader, ed. Mark J. P. Wolf and Bernard Perron. New York: Routledge.
pre_calleja_immersion_models.model_label: perceptual / psychological / social-realism immersion (operationalizing Lombard + Ditton on Myst III: Exile)
pre_calleja_immersion_models.calleja_critique_summary: Sustained critique. McMahan's Myst III analysis treats Lombard+Ditton's framework as a classification scheme rather than an analytic engine; her social-realism claims (elevators, zeppelins, page-turning) apply trivially to most digital games in similar genres, doing no game-specific work. McMahan also drifts terminologically: she treats immersion as a form of involvement, diverting it from its presence-theory transportation-connotations — a drift Calleja flags as symptomatic of the broader field-wide confusion.
pre_calleja_immersion_models.propagation_note_from_IG10: McMahan's three-fold immersion classification is wholly superseded by the six-dimensional PIM, which provides the per-game analytic resolution McMahan's scheme failed to deliver.

pre_calleja_immersion_models.full_citation: Salen, Katie, and Eric Zimmerman. 2003. Rules of Play: Game Design Fundamentals. Cambridge, MA: MIT Press.
pre_calleja_immersion_models.model_label: immersive fallacy critique + Tetris-immersibility (immersion-as-absorption applies regardless of representational mimesis)
pre_calleja_immersion_models.calleja_critique_summary: Partial endorsement and partial critique. Endorsed: the attack on the mimetic-realism imperative in game design is correct. Critiqued: the Tetris-as-immersive move (via Gorfinkel and Laramée) sidelines spatiality as a defining feature of virtual-environment immersion and conflates the absorption-sense with the transportation-sense. By calling Tetris-engagement 'immersion', Salen+Zimmerman jettison the virtual-environment specificity the term has accrued.
pre_calleja_immersion_models.propagation_note_from_IG10: Salen+Zimmerman's correct insight (immersion ≠ mimetic-realism) is preserved in the form of Calleja's resistance to fidelity-determinism (Ch.2 challenge 3). The 'immersive fallacy' framing itself is superseded by the multidimensional PIM, which separates the experiential components Salen+Zimmerman lump under 'immersion'.

pre_calleja_immersion_models.full_citation: Douglas, J. Yellowlees, and Andrew Hargadon. 2001. The Pleasures of Immersion and Engagement: Schemas, Scripts, and the Fifth Business. Digital Creativity 12 (3): 153-166.
pre_calleja_immersion_models.model_label: immersion (within-frame schema; directed interaction) vs. engagement (extra-textual critical stance; disruption of schema)
pre_calleja_immersion_models.calleja_critique_summary: Praised for recognizing the attentional continuum (conscious-to-unconscious involvement) — a recognition Calleja carries forward into Ch.3's macro/micro temporal-phase apparatus. Critiqued for collapsing ergodic vs. non-ergodic: the Balzac-Dickens-Krantz-equals-Space-Invaders move sidelines the qualitatively different forms of engagement literary works and games afford, leaving the immersion account limited to forms of involvement and missing the system-recognition feature that distinguishes transportation in game environments.
pre_calleja_immersion_models.propagation_note_from_IG10: The attentional-continuum insight is rescued under macro/micro temporal phase; the within-frame/extra-textual schema distinction itself is superseded by the multidimensional PIM.

pre_calleja_immersion_models.full_citation: Brown, Emily, and Paul Cairns. 2004. A Grounded Investigation of Immersion in Games. In CHI '04 Extended Abstracts on Human Factors in Computing Systems, 1297-1300. New York: ACM.
pre_calleja_immersion_models.model_label: engagement / engrossment / total-immersion three-degree ladder; total immersion equated with presence
pre_calleja_immersion_models.calleja_critique_summary: Productively flags continuum of attentional intensity (involvement-as-prerequisite-to-transportation), which Calleja rescues. Critiqued for mixing metaphors: levels 1-2 operate in the absorption-sense, level 3 switches to the transportation-sense — exacerbating the definitional confusion the authors had set out to resolve. The Cairns et al. (2006) follow-on quantification study inherits the mixed-metaphor flaw and also generalizes from cognitive-fatigue effects (tangram task degradation post-gameplay) not specific to games.
pre_calleja_immersion_models.propagation_note_from_IG10: The continuum-of-involvement insight survives as the macro/micro phase apparatus and as the multidimensional structure of the PIM; the three-degree ladder itself is superseded.

pre_calleja_immersion_models.full_citation: Ermi, Laura, and Frans Mäyrä. 2005. Fundamental Components of the Gameplay Experience: Analysing Immersion. In Changing Views: Worlds in Play, Proceedings of DiGRA 2005.
pre_calleja_immersion_models.model_label: multidimensional gameplay-experience model — sensory / challenge-based / imaginative immersion (empirically derived from child interviews)
pre_calleja_immersion_models.calleja_critique_summary: Major acknowledged contribution: multidimensionality + medium-specificity. Critiqued for empirical method: deriving the meaning of 'immersion' from interviews with children collapses the academic-technical sense into the colloquial sense, importing the very absorption-sense the field's progress requires disambiguating. Their account works fine if relabeled as a study of 'involvement' or 'engagement', but using 'immersion' commits the same definitional-promiscuity charge Calleja levels at the field.
pre_calleja_immersion_models.propagation_note_from_IG10: Ermi+Mäyrä's multidimensionality insight is fully absorbed: the PIM's six dimensions are an expansion of the multidimensional approach E+M initiate (with sensory ≈ kinesthetic/spatial perceptual layer, challenge-based ≈ kinesthetic+ludic, imaginative ≈ narrative+spatial). The three-mode taxonomy itself is superseded by the six-dimensional model.

pre_calleja_immersion_models_response_ty.interpretive_note: Asymmetric pattern: the two transportation-ancestors (Murray, Ryan) are critique-and-rescued — their underlying intuition (transportation, spatiality) is preserved under incorporation. The three presence-theorists (Slater+Wilbur/Slater, Witmer+Singer, Lombard+Ditton) are displaced-and-replaced — their vocabulary and analytic apparatus are not reconstituted in incorporation. The five game-studies immersion-as-absorption theorists (McMahan, Salen+Zimmerman, Douglas+Hargadon, Brown+Cairns, Ermi+Mäyrä) are critique-and-superseded — their partial insights (multidimensionality, attentional continuum, anti-mimetic-realism) are absorbed but their overall frameworks are replaced by the six-dimensional PIM. This three-way taxonomy directly mirrors Calleja's view of which prior contributions deserve preservation, which require displacement, and which contain rescuable partial insights surrounded by replaceable apparatus.

tensions.label: Absorption-metaphor vs. transportation-metaphor

claim_a.thesis: Immersion = absorption in some condition, action, interest, etc.; not medium-specific; can apply to Tetris, crossword puzzles, gardening, cooking.

claim_b.thesis: Immersion = being-present-in-another-place; medium-specific; carries virtual-environment + system-recognition specificity.

tensions.calleja_position: Both senses are legitimate but must be terminologically separated; use 'involvement' or 'absorption' for the first sense, reserve 'immersion' (or, better, a new term — incorporation) for the second. The conflation is the first of the four challenges.

tensions.label: Fidelity-determinism vs. interpretation-and-agency

claim_a.thesis: Hardware-fidelity drives presence; form is separable from content; a high-fidelity sound system makes you feel present in the theatre regardless of whether the music engages you.

claim_b.thesis: Interpretation, agency, and prior lived experience are constitutive of presence; the form/content partition cannot be cleanly drawn because interpretive apparatus participates in form-perception itself. Someone who has never attended a concert may not feel 'present' regardless of fidelity.

tensions.calleja_position: Reject fidelity-determinism. High-fidelity hardware enhances intensity but cannot in itself create presence. The Heidegger p.21 cite supplies the everyday-vs-disrupted comportment distinction that underwrites the rejection.

tensions.label: Ergodic/non-ergodic media equivalence vs. categorical difference

claim_a.thesis: Presence and immersion are experiential phenomena that can occur uniformly across ergodic and non-ergodic media; the same psychological apparatus operates whether one is in a virtual environment or reading a novel.

claim_b.thesis: Ergodic media require nontrivial player effort and feature system-recognition of the player's location and actions; non-ergodic media do not. Extending presence-concepts across this divide stretches presence to cover 'an entirely noetic phenomenon' and loses the original technological-affordance specificity.

tensions.calleja_position: Endorse the categorical-difference side. This is challenge 2 of the four challenges and motivates the avatar-anchoring claim.

tensions.label: Monolithic on/off accounts of immersion vs. graded-continuum accounts

claim_a.thesis: Immersion/presence is a single phenomenon to be operationally defined and quantitatively measured.

claim_b.thesis: Immersion is composed of multiple experiential components distributed on a continuum of attentional intensity; binary measurement is inadequate.

tensions.calleja_position: Endorse the continuum side. This is challenge 4 and seeds Ch.3's macro/micro temporal-phase distinction.

game_loci.analytic_function: Paradigm of immersion-as-absorption WITHOUT spatial habitation. Used by Salen+Zimmerman (via Gorfinkel) to argue immersion is not tied to mimetic-realism. Calleja deploys Tetris against itself: agrees Tetris is engaging-in-the-absorption-sense but denies it instances the transportation-sense, because (a) the player is not embodied in a single in-game entity, (b) the environment is shown in totality on one screen, (c) there is no continuous spatial navigation. Co-anchors Figure 2.1.

Paradigm of immersion-as-transportation WITH spatial habitation. Player is anchored via avatar in a specific location; game world reacts to her; world functions as 'metaphorically habitable environment'. Co-anchors Figure 2.1. Original Half-Life also cited in industry-promotional rhetoric of immersive storytelling (p.25).

McMahan's analytic foil. Used by Calleja to show how Lombard+Ditton's six-categories framework, when operationalized for analysis, degenerates into descriptive feature-listing that fails to elucidate game-specific affordances.

Used to make the point that even open-ended virtual worlds remain designed environments — players are not, at any point, confused about that designed nature. Counter-evidence to Ijsselsteijn+Riva's equivalence-claim.
Member of the non-habitable game class alongside Tetris and Eliss; no avatar-anchoring, no continuous spatial navigation.
Member of the non-habitable game class; touch-control planet-manipulation game with totality-on-screen and no in-world embodiment.

Douglas+Hargadon's example of cognitive-load immersion; Calleja deploys it to show how the Balzac-Dickens-Krantz-equals-Space-Invaders move collapses ergodic vs. non-ergodic and loses the system-recognition feature.
Specimen of industry-promotional rhetoric: 'graphics in Conan immerses you into a world as never before seen' — used by Calleja to illustrate the marketing-grade 'immersive' adjective.
Specimen of industry-promotional rhetoric: 'immersive game world where the streets are your menus' — used alongside Conan.
Specimen of industry-promotional rhetoric: 'pounding action and continuous, immersive storytelling'.

heidegger_p21_capture.in_text_context: Calleja, having just quoted Slater 2003's quadraphonic-orchestra example at the foot of p.20, opens p.21 by arguing that fidelity-determinism underweights interpretation and agency in constituting a sense of presence. He then makes three connected claims (paraphrastically): interpretation need not be conscious; most environmental interactions rely on internalized knowledge of how aspects of the environment work; when an experience resists ready interpretation, our comportment becomes critically removed and we must actively think about what we are doing. The parenthetical '(Heidegger, 1993)' is attached to the last claim with no further explication.
heidegger_p21_capture.calleja_use: The Heidegger reference functions as authorization for the everyday-vs-disrupted comportment distinction. Calleja uses it to ground the claim that interpretive apparatus is constitutive (not merely modulatory) of presence — and therefore that fidelity-determinism must fail.
heidegger_p21_capture.exegetical_depth: Single-sentence parenthetical cite. No engagement with Sein und Zeit, Dasein, In-der-Welt-sein, ready-to-hand/Zuhandenheit, the everyday/Eigentlichkeit distinction, or any specific argument from Question Concerning Technology beyond the broad gesture at technology-and-comportment.
heidegger_p21_capture.what_calleja_does_not_do: Calleja does not name the structure he invokes (one would natively gloss it as the Heideggerian shift from zuhanden to vorhanden — but Calleja does not use that vocabulary). He does not identify which Heidegger essay the 1993 [1977] volume he names. He does not engage Aristotelian-Heideggerian time-phenomenology (which his macro/micro temporal-phase distinction at Ch.3 would invite). The reference operates as a single one-sentence philosophical authorization rather than as a sustained ontological grounding.
heidegger_p21_capture.implication_for_dissertation: This is the SOLE ontological-grounding-related cite in the entire book (per cite_check.heidegger in manifest.json). All other ontological-grounding edges (to BCAP, Phantasia Cluster, Bowin AMT, etc.) remain anticipatory-projection relative to Calleja's text. The p.21 cite is, however, the closest Calleja comes to phenomenological-hermeneutic register in the volume, and so it functions as the dissertation's one text-anchored proxy for Layer A integration.

notes: Densest-citation chapter in the volume — 37 distinct interlocutors captured. The asymmetric response-type pattern (2 critique-and-rescue + 3 displace-and-replace + 5 critique-and-supersede) is the key Phase 3 input for the debate-map deliverable: the dissertation Manual will draw its prior-model analysis directly from this taxonomy. Murray-as-absorbed-not-refused (per IG-10 propagation, p.172) is incorporated as the canonical critique-and-rescue exemplar; Ryan follows the same pattern. The presence-theory triple (Slater/Witmer+Singer/Lombard+Ditton) is the canonical displace-and-replace cluster — Calleja preserves none of their vocabulary or analytic apparatus under incorporation. The game-studies-immersion-as-absorption pentad (McMahan/Salen+Zimmerman/Douglas+Hargadon/Brown+Cairns/Ermi+Mäyrä) is the critique-and-supersede cluster — Calleja absorbs specific insights from each (multidimensionality from E+M; attentional continuum from D+H and B+C; anti-mimetic-realism from S+Z; the failure-of-feature-classification diagnostic from McMahan) but supersedes the overall frameworks with the six-dimensional PIM.
